explanations.answer: Which of them should be considered the greatest
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Luke says a dispute arose among the disciples as to which of them should be considered the greatest. Picture a group chat that went sideways, except everybody is sitting at the same table. I think that table got quiet in a hurry.

explanations.answer: Which of them should lead the Passover prayer
explanations.explanation: Good guess for a Passover table, but the text doesn't say a word about a prayer fight. What it says is that the dispute was about which of them should be considered the greatest. Nobody in this passage is fighting over who gets the microphone. I once argued with my own cookie timer and lost, so I respect a good argument, but this wasn't that one.

explanations.answer: Which of them should go out to buy supplies
explanations.explanation: I get it, somebody always has to make the run. But the passage never mentions a supply run. The dispute was about which of them should be considered the greatest. Nobody was fighting to be the one holding the shopping list, friend.

That's right, baker. Jesus tells them, “But you shall not be like them.” The kings of the Gentiles, the nations outside Israel, lord it over people, and the disciples are not to follow that example. Jesus gives them a different way to live, and He's about to say what it looks like.

Not quite, friend. The text says Jesus does tell them this: “But you shall not be like them.” The them is the kings of the Gentiles, the nations outside Israel, who lord it over people. So the answer is True, and a different way of leading is coming right behind it.

Serves is it, baker. Jesus says, “…and the one who leads like the one who serves.” That's the opposite of what the kings of the Gentiles do. Leading by serving is like the head of a bakery who stays late to scrub the pans. I know a stamper who would look pretty good doing it.

I see why you'd pick it, since commanding sounds like what leaders do. But Jesus has just said the disciples shall not be like the kings who lord it over people. What He actually says is, “…and the one who leads like the one who serves.” Commanding is the very thing He's steering them away from.

Deciding does sound like a leader's job, friend. But Jesus doesn't say that here. He says, “…and the one who leads like the one who serves.” Leaders get a different picture, and it comes with an apron.

Close, because Jesus does bring up the one who reclines. He asks who is greater, the one who reclines at the table or the one who serves, and says it is the one who reclines. But then He says, “But I am among you as one who serves.” So He says He is the one who serves, which makes this False.

Yes, baker. Jesus asks who is greater, the one who reclines or the one who serves, and agrees it's the one who reclines. Then He turns it around: “But I am among you as one who serves.” The One at the table is the One serving. That sure beats any of us fighting over a seat.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, “And I bestow on you a kingdom, just as My Father has bestowed one on Me.” The kingdom He gives them comes the same way His own did. Think of Him passing down a recipe He was given Himself.
Nope, friend. Jesus doesn't say the people gave Him a kingdom. He says, “…just as My Father has bestowed one on Me.” It comes from His Father, not from a vote.

The prophets show up a lot in Scripture, so I get the guess. But in this verse, Jesus says the kingdom was bestowed on Him by His Father: “…just as My Father has bestowed one on Me.” The prophets aren't named here. Hold onto that line, because it ties His kingdom and theirs together.

Table it is, baker. Jesus says, “…so that you may eat and drink at My table in My kingdom…” A table is a place where people sit together and stay a while. It's my favorite kind of furniture, and I say that as someone who works at a counter.

An altar sounds serious, and I see the pull. But Jesus says they will eat and drink at His table. The line is, “…so that you may eat and drink at My table in My kingdom…” A table is where people sit down together.

A gate is where people walk through, not where they sit down. Jesus says the disciples will eat and drink at His table: “…so that you may eat and drink at My table in My kingdom…” That's a seat, friend, not a doorway.

explanations.answer: Judging the twelve tribes of Israel
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus says they will “…sit on thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” Not long after a fight over who's greatest, He tells them where they're headed. I think that's one humbling day at the table.

explanations.answer: Teaching the nations of the earth
explanations.explanation: Teaching the nations is a good-sounding job, but it isn't what Jesus says here. He says they will sit on thrones, “judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” That's the job in this verse. Always check the line, friend, because it keeps your guesses honest.

explanations.answer: Counting the people of every land
explanations.explanation: Counting every person sounds like a full-time job and a half. But it isn't what Jesus says. He says they will sit on thrones, “judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” No clipboard in the text, baker.

explanations.answer: Prayed that his faith will not fail
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Jesus says to Simon, “But I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith will not fail.” Simon is the disciple Jesus also named Peter. Satan, the devil, has asked to sift them like wheat, and Jesus has already prayed for him. That's Jesus covering Simon before the trouble even starts.

explanations.answer: Sent an angel to stand guard over him
explanations.explanation: An angel on guard duty is a nice picture, but the text doesn't say it. What Jesus says is, “But I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith will not fail.” Simon is the disciple Jesus also named Peter. The thing Jesus names is His prayer.

explanations.answer: Told him to hide until morning comes
explanations.explanation: Hiding would be the cookie-under-the-couch approach, and I've seen it. But Jesus doesn't tell Simon to hide. He says, “But I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith will not fail.” Simon is the disciple Jesus also named Peter. And Jesus follows it by giving him a job.

explanations.answer: Even to prison and to death
explanations.explanation: That's what he says, baker. Peter, the disciple Jesus called Simon, answers, “Lord, I am ready to go with You even to prison and to death.” That's a big promise to make at a table. Next Jesus will give Peter an answer he didn't expect.

explanations.answer: Even through the storm and the sea
explanations.explanation: A storm and a sea do show up in other stories about the disciples, so I see the mix-up. But here, Peter, the disciple Jesus called Simon, says, “I am ready to go with You even to prison and to death.” No water in this one. It's a bigger promise than any boat ride.

explanations.answer: Even into the desert and the wild
explanations.explanation: Desert and wild country are good guesses for a story like this, but Peter doesn't say them. Peter, the disciple Jesus called Simon, says, “I am ready to go with You even to prison and to death.” Those are the two places he names. Friend, that's serious loyalty talk.

explanations.answer: Deny three times that he knows Jesus
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Jesus says, “I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow today until you have denied three times that you know Me.” It's hard to hear right after Peter's big promise. I think that one stings, and I won't joke about it.

explanations.answer: Leave Jerusalem before the sun comes up
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't say anything about Peter leaving a city. What He says is, “…the rooster will not crow today until you have denied three times that you know Me.” The rooster is the clock in this verse. And what happens before it is denying Jesus three times.

explanations.answer: Go back home to Galilee tonight
explanations.explanation: Going home would be a different story, friend, and it isn't the one Jesus tells. He says, “I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow today until you have denied three times that you know Me.” The thing before the rooster is denial. Three times, not a trip.

Yes, baker. Jesus asks, “When I sent you out without purse or bag or sandals, did you lack anything?” and they answer, “Nothing.” Even with empty hands, they had what they needed. That's a one-word answer you don't see every day.

Bread is a natural thing to name, but the disciples don't name any food. They answer, “Nothing.” Jesus asks if they lacked anything when He sent them out without purse or bag or sandals, and the answer is a flat none.

Shelter feels like something you'd miss on the road, so I see the guess. But they didn't name a single thing. Jesus asks, “…did you lack anything?” and they answer, “Nothing.” That's the whole answer.

Not quite, friend. Jesus says the opposite: “Now, however, the one with a purse should take it, and likewise a bag…” He's not saying to leave it behind. Back when He sent them out, they went without purse or bag. Now He says take them.

Yes, baker. Jesus says, “Now, however, the one with a purse should take it, and likewise a bag…” That's a change from the time He sent them out with no purse or bag. Things are different now, and He tells them so plainly.
Buy is it, baker. Jesus says, “…and the one without a sword should sell his cloak and buy one.” He tells them to sell the cloak to get it. That's a big trade, and I'd be asking questions.

Borrowing would be easier on the wallet, but it isn't what Jesus says. He says the one without a sword should “…sell his cloak and buy one.” Sell the cloak, buy the sword. No lending in the verse, friend.
Forging a sword takes a blacksmith, and I only know ovens. That isn't what Jesus says anyway. He says, “…sell his cloak and buy one.” The text sticks to buying.

True, baker. Jesus says, “For I tell you that this Scripture must be fulfilled in Me: ‘And He was numbered with the transgressors.’ For what is written about Me is reaching its fulfillment.” The words He points to come from the prophet Isaiah (Isaiah 53:12). He says the writing about Him is reaching its fulfillment.

Not this time, friend. Jesus does say it: “For what is written about Me is reaching its fulfillment.” He's pointing to a Scripture from the prophet Isaiah, “And He was numbered with the transgressors.” (Isaiah 53:12) So the answer is True.
Not quite, baker. The disciples say, “Look, Lord, here are two swords.” Jesus answers, “That is enough.” He doesn't tell them to go get more. So the answer is False.

Yes, baker. When the disciples say, “Look, Lord, here are two swords,” Jesus answers, “That is enough.” He doesn't send them off for more. His words end the conversation, and the story still has more to tell.
